question.prompt:
Right triangle \(ACD\) with right angle at \(C\) is constructed outwards on the hypotenuse \(\overline{AC}\) of isosceles right triangle \(ABC\) with leg length \(1,\) as shown, so that the two triangles have equal perimeters. What is \(\sin(2\angle BAD)?\)

[Figure 1](figures/2019_AMC_12B_Q12_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
The equal perimeters are useful because the common side \(AC\) cancels, giving a simple sum for the two unknown sides.

[Figure 1](figures/2019_AMC_12B_Q12_question_fig1.svg)

Since \(AB=BC=1\) and \(\angle ABC=90^\circ\), the Pythagorean theorem gives \(AC=\sqrt2\). Write \(CD=x\) and \(AD=y\), where both lengths are positive. Equal perimeters and the right angle at \(C\) give
\[
x+y=2,
\qquad y^2-x^2=AC^2=2.
\]
Factoring the second equation and using the first yields
\[
(y-x)(y+x)=2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
2(y-x)=2.
\]
Thus \(y-x=1\), and combining the sum and difference gives
\[
x=\frac12,\qquad y=\frac32.
\]
These positive lengths satisfy the original perimeter and right-triangle relations.

Let \(\theta=\angle CAD\), which is acute. The right triangle \(ACD\) gives
\[
\sin\theta=\frac{CD}{AD}=\frac13.
\]
The acute angles of the isosceles right triangle \(ABC\) are equal and sum to \(90^\circ\), so \(\angle BAC=45^\circ\). Because \(ACD\) is constructed outward, rays \(AB\) and \(AD\) lie on opposite sides of \(AC\). Hence \(\angle BAD=45^\circ+\theta\).

This angle sum turns the requested sine into a cosine double angle:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sin(2\angle BAD)
&=\sin(90^\circ+2\theta)\\
&=\cos(2\theta)\\
&=1-2\sin^2\theta\\
&=1-\frac29=\boxed{\frac79}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The answer is choice D.
solutions.title: Use the 45-degree angle

solutions.explanation:
Coordinates along the legs of \(ABC\) let us compute the sine and cosine of \(\angle BAD\) directly from the horizontal and vertical displacements to \(D\).

[Figure 1](figures/2019_AMC_12B_Q12_question_fig1.svg)

First, \(AC=\sqrt2\) by the Pythagorean theorem. Put \(CD=x>0\) and \(AD=y>0\). Cancelling \(AC\) from the equal perimeters gives \(x+y=2\), while the right triangle \(ACD\) gives \(y^2-x^2=2\). Therefore
\[
2(y-x)=(y+x)(y-x)=2,
\]
so \(y-x=1\). Consequently \(CD=1/2\) and \(AD=3/2\), which satisfy both original relations.

Place
\[
A=(0,0),\qquad B=(1,0),\qquad C=(1,1).
\]
The line \(AC\) has slope \(1\), so its perpendicular through \(C\) has slope \(-1\) and equation \(x+y=2\). The outward side is the side opposite \(B\), so we can write
\[
D=(1-t,1+t),\qquad t>0.
\]
Using \(CD=1/2\), we obtain
\[
t^2+t^2=\frac14
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 t=\frac{\sqrt2}{4},
\]
where the positive root is required by the outward construction. In particular, \(0<t<1\), so both coordinates of \(D\) are positive.

Let \(\alpha=\angle BAD\). Since \(AB\) points along the positive horizontal axis and \(AD=3/2\), right-triangle ratios give
\[
\sin\alpha=\frac{1+t}{3/2},
\qquad
\cos\alpha=\frac{1-t}{3/2}.
\]
The sine double-angle identity now gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sin(2\alpha)
&=2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha\\
&=\frac{2(1-t^2)}{(3/2)^2}\\
&=\frac{2(1-1/8)}{9/4}
=\boxed{\frac79}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The answer is choice D.
solutions.title: Compute sine and cosine from coordinates
